study.title: Proverbs 6: prudence, diligence, integrity, and fidelity
study.overview: Proverbs 6 brings together practical and spiritual warnings about very concrete areas of life: reckless financial commitments, laziness, planned malice, things that the Lord hates, the importance of family education and the danger of sexual immorality. The chapter shows that biblical wisdom does not separate devotion of daily life: the fear of the Lord appears both in the way of dealing with money and work and in the way of speaking, desire and keeping the conjugal covenant. Teaching is repeated strongly because moral and social ruin usually begins with small concessions.

outline.title: Beware of reckless guarantees
outline.explanation: The text warns against becoming someone else's guarantor, especially lightly. The proposed solution is urgent and humiliated: getting rid of the obligation before it destroys the house and freedom. Gravity is compared to the escape of an animal trapped in trap.

outline.title: Laziness, active wickedness, and what God hates
outline.explanation: The ant is used as an example of diligence without needing external surveillance. In contrast, the perverse man is described by deceptive gestures, the planner heart of evil and sowing of conflicts. The section culminates in a list of seven things that the Lord hates, centered on pride, lies, violence and discord.

outline.title: The word as a guide and adultery as self-destruction
outline.explanation: The child must keep the commandment of the parents because faithful instruction guides, protects and corrects. Then the chapter again warns against the adulterous woman, showing that seduction begins in the heart and ends in real damage. Adultery is described as a lack of understanding, destruction of one's own soul and permanent shame, without the possibility of compensation that removes the offense to the outraged husband.

study.context: The chapter belongs to the collection of proverbs linked to the practical wisdom attributed to Solomon. The scores provided highlight that teaching is focused on everyday life: finance, work, human relations, family discipline and sexual purity. There is not enough base, in the notes, to broaden with historical details beyond that; the focus of the text is pedagogical and moral.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter presents God as the one who sees and judges not only external acts, but also intentions, habits and desires. Biblical wisdom is highly concrete: it protects from financial ruin, idleness, lies, verbal and physical violence, and sexual infidelity. The moral contrast is strong: the righteous hears instruction and walks in light; the perverse plot, seduces and destroys. The list of the seven things hated by God shows that he especially rejects pride, falsehood, innocent blood, and division among brethren. In dealing with adultery as self-destruction, the text shows that sexual sin is not only a breakage of rule, but deep wound against one's own person, against others and against God's moral order. The confessional interpretations in the notes also point out that the wisdom of God protects the present, not only the future life.

scholarViews.insight: The guarantee by another person is too high a risk, capable of leading to financial ruin; therefore the text has to be rid of the obligation without delay.
The ant teaches the lazy diligence and foresight, showing that the lack of effort leads to poverty.
Adultery is an injury without real compensation; gifts cannot satisfy the offense or erase dishonor.

questions: In which areas of life have I made commitments without prudence, relying too much on my own strength or the good will of others?
What do my attitudes reveal: diligence and discipline, or laziness and postponement that tend to produce spiritual and practical poverty?
Have I treated purity, honesty and peace among brothers as priorities of the Lord, or as secondary matters?
study.practice: Practice three concrete movements this week: review financial and relational commitments that may be reckless; establish a simple routine of faithful and persevering work, learning from the ant; and protect the heart with the instruction of God, avoiding conversations, images and fantasies that feed infidelity, lie or discord. Memorize especially verses 20 to 23 as a daily decision filter.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not base the accuracy of additional historical details, nor to state more than the chapter itself says about specific customs. In Proverbs 6:35, the notes of Tyndale and Adam Clarke refer to the jealous husband and the impossibility of compensation, but it is not possible, safely from the notes, to develop more than this without extrapolating.
